speaker: evander
text: Good morning to both of you. We're here for an oral argument session of the Fifth District Court of Appeal. First case this morning is Middleton versus Middleton, 20-1659. I'm Judge Evander. I'll be presiding today. I'm joined on the panel by Judge Edwards and Judge Harris. Each have 20 minutes aside for oral argument. Mr. Bogdanoff, if you want to tell me how much time you wish to reserve for rebuttal, I'll try to help you, but there should be a clock in the corner there. text: May it please the court, good morning. I'm John Bogdanoff for the former wife, Sharon Middleton. The trial court erred in this case.

speaker: johnbogdanoff
text: The trial court erred in several material respects in connection with this action by the former wife to modify her alimony. In denying the former wife's motion for attorney's fees, the court failed to consider the motion as required under the correct legal standard, which is chapter 61. In fact, 6116 applies to modification proceedings, and it involves the need and ability to pay standard. The trial court here, in discussing attorney's fees at the end of its order, referred to the fact that the wife had not prevailed on a substantial issue. We believe that under the circumstances, at the very least, a reversal is required for reconsideration of the former wife's motion for attorney's fees under the appropriate standard. Furthermore, in denying fees, the trial court determined erroneously that the former husband had contributed over $20,000 towards her attorney's fees. As the former husband has acknowledged, that amount was only $10,000. And thus, the trial court's denial of attorney's fees is also based on a finding, which is contrary to the undisputed evidence in the case. More impactful, however, were the reversible errors the court made in denying the former wife's request for an increase in her $3,000 a month alimony. The court correctly found that the former wife had suffered a substantial change in circumstances when, in 2016, her health insurance premiums increased from $360 to just over $2,000 on a monthly basis. The court determined that was a substantial change. But then the court erroneously concluded that no increase in alimony was warranted, finding that the former wife could avail herself of a $383,000 inheritance that she had received from her father in 2016. Again, this finding that this $383,000 was available to the former wife is totally unsupported by any substantial competent evidence. The only evidence in the case was that the former wife had used this money in 2016 to pay off a Merrill Lynch loan that she had taken out in 2011 and that this $383,000 was no longer available. There was no dispute.

speaker: edwards
text: Counsel, there's no dispute that she received the money, is there?

speaker: johnbogdanoff
text: No, there's no dispute.

text: She chose to use the money to basically wind up with a mortgage-free house, in part?

text: No, not entirely. She used the money to pay off attorney's fees, as her brother had testified in this case, and he was a witness for the former husband. She had incurred in excess of a million dollars in attorney's fees in connection with this litigation. The trial court denied her attorney's fees in the 2009 divorce decree, and so she was left responsible for her own attorney's fees. So she testified that part of the Merrill Lynch loan was to pay attorney's fees, part was to pay expenses, that she was continuing to incur that were in excess of the alimony she was receiving, and that a small amount of the money did go towards obtaining a residence, a home. But she had received $377,000, I believe, in the equitable distribution. She used the bulk of that to acquire a home, but she did supplement that a bit with the Merrill Lynch money.

speaker: edwards

speaker: johnbogdanoff

She enjoyed a decent lifestyle during the marriage.

speaker: evander
text: I'll ask you this. Since the trial judge found that the former wife had not met her burden to show that her health condition had deteriorated such that she could not work, and therefore kept the imputed income, was there any evidence as to what health insurance premiums would be or would be available, the amount of those premiums, if she had, in fact, sought and obtained employment? speaker: johnbogdanoff
text: Well, there was no evidence as to the availability of health insurance in the event she had a 40-hour-a-week job. So the answer to that is there was no evidence. The trial judge did find that the $2,000-a-month increase in her premiums was a substantial change in circumstance. So the judge did not find that this was an unwarranted or improper or somehow increase that was not appropriate. But what he did find, unfortunately, was that somehow this $383,000 was still available to pay this increase, to pay her attorney's fees, and to also live on in the future. And that money, there was no substantial competent evidence that that money exists and is available for her to pay these health insurance premiums. So the court did find the premiums were appropriate, but then failed to adjust the alimony appropriately to allow for an increase, given that substantial change in circumstances. The additional issue involved relates to her substantial deterioration in her health. She presented overwhelming evidence from three doctors, from a physical therapist, from a vocational rehabilitation expert, that her health had substantially deteriorated. She was diagnosed in 2018 with rheumatoid arthritis. She had a 50% decrease in her functionality based on medical tests. That was testified to. And that had occurred since 2009. She had a 1% hand functionality, which was diagnosed in 2016, which meant that she can only do 1% of what a typical person could do with her hands. So these things were diagnosed well after the divorce decree was entered in 2009. And there were substantial evidence that she was able.

speaker: elizabethsianoharris

speaker: johnbogdanoff
text: If he had substantial competent evidence to do so, but there is no substantial evidence.

text: Well, if they say a picture is worth a thousand words, what about the videos here that seem to completely contradict her version of what's going on these days?

text: The video actually confirmed what the testimony was. The video showed it was several snippets. text: Well, he can look, obviously, yeah, he can look at it, but the question is, does it confirm her ability to work 40 hours a week, or is it more confirmatory of the fact that she, over short, minimal periods of time, the longest video was 18 minutes, that she's capable of functioning? And the answer was, she's capable of functioning over that short period of time, but there's no showing that she's capable of working 40 hours a week, given the testimony that she presented and the opinions of her experts that, at most, she can work just a couple of days a week for short periods of time, which, again...

speaker: edwards

speaker: johnbogdanoff
text: There was some evidence that, on bad days, she did have difficulty walking up stairs. You know, there was testimony she had good days and bad days. Obviously, the judge can look at the video, but just like the Florida Board of Bar Governors' work that she did, it was five hours a week that she worked for the Board of Governors of the bar, again, confirming that she's able to do... So, you know, the court, again, in looking at the video, said, well, she didn't appear to be, you know, completely and basically, you know, enfeebled, which is not the standard. The standard is, was there a substantial change in circumstances, deterioration in her health? She presented overwhelming evidence of that, and as a result of that, that she's no longer able to work full-time, which is what the court had imputed income in based on 40 hours a week back in 2012, and the answer is yes, and there was no evidence that showed otherwise. All the evidence that was presented actually would seem to be confirmatory of this limited ability of her to work and this substantial change in circumstances.

speaker: evander
text: Mr. Baumann, if a judge overall finds a witness to be somewhat less than credible, and the doctors are relying, at least in part, on her subjective complaints and reaching their opinions, can the trial court properly consider that in deciding whether or not she's met her burden of proof?

speaker: evander

So the judge made a finding, but the judge's finding is simply not supported by the evidence, and he applied the standard of so debilitated instead of, was there a substantial change in your, or deterioration in your health? One thing I also wanted to point out, your honors, with respect to the health insurance premiums, counsels may have misspoke a little bit about the numbers. So when it comes back to the ultimate question, which is, did the wife meet her burden of proof in establishing that there had been a substantial, unanticipated change in circumstances, we submit the trial court got it right. To the extent that counsel complained about the attorney's fee number of 20,000 versus 10,000, I would submit that that's either a clerical or de minimis matter.

speaker: evander

speaker: evander

text: Thank you, Your Honor. So again, the judge's determinations just are not supported by competent substantial evidence, whether it be that somehow the attorney's fees are covered by the inheritance, past and future health insurance premium, monthly health insurance premiums are absorbed by the inheritance. It just, it doesn't wash. And the judgment in that regard is not supported by competent substantial evidence. One additional, or a couple of additional points. Dr. Schutte was a physical therapist. He acknowledged he was not competent to offer an opinion as to employability. He said, that's up to the referring physician who was Dr. Gabor. Dr. Gabor repudiated Schutte's testimony and said that based on the objective evidence in the case, that the former wife had a deterioration in her health such that she could only work a couple of days a month. That was his opinion. And he repudiated Schutte's opinion that she was able to do light sedentary work full time. So that, again, is not competent substantial evidence to support the trial judge's decision. There were, this was not a case of mere subjective evidence of a deterioration in health. We had a 1% hand functionality test in 2016, a 50% decrease in functional capacity since 2009. Rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis in 2018. These are not subjective complaints. These were objective, this is objective evidence that was testified to by the physicians. Yes, in 2009, there was an indication that the wife's health was not going to substantially improve, but there was not a determination that it would substantially deteriorate. And nothing that the trial court said, I'd refer to it as the three pillars, the board of governor's evidence, the surveillance video, and physical therapist Schutte, not one of those pillars constitutes competent substantial evidence that she's able to work 40 hours a week. So we would ask the court to consider that, also consider the fact that the trial court referenced the wife as not being so debilitated when that's not the standard.
